resources.string: The derivative of a constant is zero
The derivative of the variable is one
Write the power with base e
Change the base of the logarithm
Integrate the Gaussian function (it gives the error function)
Integrate sin(x)/x (it gives the sine integral Si)
Integrate cos(x)/x (it gives the cosine integral Ci)
Integrate eˣ/x (it gives the exponential integral Ei)
Put the values into the density of the normal distribution
Write the normal probability with the error function
Scale the quantile of the standard normal distribution
Put the values into the density of the t distribution
Put the values into the density of the chi-square distribution
Put the values into the binomial probability
Add the binomial probabilities of 0 up to k
Put the values into the Poisson probability
Add the Poisson probabilities of 0 up to k
Write out the sum with its terms calculated
Multiply the matching components and add them
Work out the cross product component by component
The length of a vector is the root of the sum of its squared components
The angle follows from the dot product and the lengths of the two vectors
Project the vector onto the other one
Divide the vector by its length
Two vectors are equal when their components are: one equation for each component
Put the parameter into its line to get the point where the lines meet
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus
Take the root of a negative number
Give the fractions a common denominator
Write the tangent as sine over cosine
Take the reciprocal of both sides: secant ↔ cosine, cosecant ↔ sine, cotangent ↔ tangent
Write the secant, cosecant and cotangent with sine and cosine
Apply the inverse hyperbolic function (for cosh and sech the negative value is a solution too)
The exact value of a special angle (unit circle)
The logarithm of a power of its base is the exponent
A power of the base with its logarithm as the exponent is the number
The root of a fraction: the root of the numerator over the root of the denominator
Divide the polynomials: the quotient and a fraction with a lower degree
Integrate by parts twice: the same integral comes back, solve for it
Write the square of the sine or cosine with the double angle
The square of the sine plus the square of the cosine of the same angle is 1
The square of the secant minus the square of the tangent of the same angle is 1
The square of the cosecant minus the square of the cotangent of the same angle is 1
The square of the hyperbolic cosine minus the square of the hyperbolic sine of the same number is 1
A function times its reciprocal function of the same angle is 1
The exact value of a hyperbolic function (at 0, or at a logarithm)
An odd power of the sine or cosine: keep one factor, write the rest with the other function
Remove the root from the denominator: multiply numerator and denominator by it
Divide both sides by a negative number: the inequality sign turns around
Multiply both sides by a negative number: the inequality sign turns around
Swap the sides: the inequality sign turns around
Everything to the left: compare with 0
The sign can only change where the two sides are equal (the left side minus the right side is 0)
…or where it is not defined: a denominator is 0, or a root or logarithm begins
These points divide the line into intervals; the sign is the same inside each one
Test one value in each interval (and each point): where the inequality holds is the solution
Combine the logarithms: the sum is the logarithm of the product, the difference of the quotient
Equal logarithms of the same base: the insides are equal
Write the squared sine with the cosine (or the other way round)
The root of a square is the absolute value
Write the double angle with the single angle
Combine sine and cosine into one sine, with R = √(a² + b²) and tan φ = b/a (π added if a < 0)
Write the percent as a fraction: a percent is hundredths
Write the mixed number as an improper fraction
Multiply the numerators and the denominators
Take the largest square factor out of the root
Write the power as a root
Write the power as a fraction
Raise each factor to the power
Factor and cancel the common factor
Sine over cosine is the tangent
Integrate one over the root of a square plus a number: the inverse hyperbolic sine
Integrate one over the root of a square minus a number: a logarithm (the same for positive and negative x)
Split the numerator into the derivative of the denominator and a constant
Complete the square in the denominator
Taylor polynomial: wanted is the polynomial Tₙ of degree n that has the same value and the same first n derivatives as f at x = a. Near a it approximates f, the better the higher n is
Write down the Taylor formula up to degree n: for each k from 0 to n, the k-th derivative at a, divided by k!, times (x − a)^k
Differentiate f again and again, up to the n-th derivative: each one is the derivative of the one before
Put x = a into f and into each derivative
Put the values into the Taylor formula
Work out the factorials and simplify each term; the terms with the value 0 drop out
Take the square root of both sides
Split off a factor: if P(r) = 0, then (x − r) is a factor
Take the root of both sides
Take the logarithm of both sides
The function repeats: add whole periods, 2π for sine and cosine, π for tangent
Divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of the denominator
Get the trigonometric function on its own
Inside one period the solution is one interval or two, found from the inverse function; every period gives the same ones again, 2kπ later (kπ for tangent and cotangent)
Now the inside is x: subtract and divide on every part
Sine and cosine are always between −1 and 1
Every term has degree 2: divide by x² and write t = y/x (x = 0 is no solution of this equation, it is checked on its own)
The inside of |…| is positive or negative: |g| is g where g ≥ 0 and −g where g < 0. Each case is an equation of its own
Solve this case: its solutions only count where its condition holds
Each inequality is solved on its own first
All of them have to hold: only the values that are in every solution are left
Logarithms to the same base: a sum is the logarithm of the product, a difference the logarithm of the quotient, and n·log a is log(aⁿ)
ln a / ln b is the logarithm of a to the base b (change of base)
√a − b is ∞ − ∞ here: multiplying by the conjugate (the same with the other sign) turns it into a quotient
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²: the roots disappear from the numerator
If the exponent goes to ∞, eᵍ goes to ∞; if it goes to −∞, eᵍ goes to 0
Close to the point on this side the inside of |…| keeps its sign, so |g| = g (positive) or −g (negative)
Terms that go to 0 vanish (a variable in a denominator, e^(−x)), and arctan of a growing number is ±π/2
The limit of a constant is the constant
The highest power grows without bound
A denominator that grows without bound: the quotient goes to 0
Substitute u = 1/x: then u goes to 0
The base goes to 1 and the exponent to ∞: write the power with e and take the limit of the exponent
The limit is e to the power of that limit
Find the zeros of the polynomial (rational root theorem): each zero r gives a factor (x − r)
To use a matrix or vector again, store it with := (long press on =), for example v := [vector]
The determinant of a 2×2 matrix: the product of the diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal
Expand the determinant along a row or column: each entry times the determinant of what is left when its row and column are crossed out, the signs alternate
The inverse of a 2×2 matrix: swap the diagonal, change the signs of the other two entries, and divide by the determinant
Write the matrix next to the identity matrix: row operations that turn the left part into the identity turn the right part into the inverse
Swap two rows to get a pivot that is not 0
Divide the row by its pivot so that the pivot is 1
Add or subtract a multiple of the pivot row to make the other entries in this column 0
Row reduction: row operations turn every pivot into 1 and the other entries in its column into 0 (reduced row echelon form)
The eigenvalues λ are where A − λ·I is not invertible: the determinant of A − λ·I is 0
An eigenvector v of this eigenvalue solves (A − λ·I)·v = 0: reduce the rows
Free variables are set to 1 and 0; v is scaled to whole numbers (any multiple is an eigenvector as well)
The eigenvalues, each with an eigenvector
The left part is the identity matrix: the right part is the inverse
Multiply the matrices: each entry is a row of the first times a column of the second
A number times a matrix: it multiplies every entry
Add the matrices entry by entry
Subtract the matrices entry by entry
A power of a matrix is the matrix multiplied by itself
One bound is infinite: the antiderivative at t instead of at the bound, and the limit as t goes to infinity
The denominator goes to 0 and the numerator does not: the quotient grows without bound, the signs say which way
The logarithm of a number that goes to 0⁺ goes to −∞
It is 0·∞: write the product as a quotient first
It is 0/0 or ∞/∞: apply l\'Hôpital\'s rule
A fraction is zero if its numerator is zero
Two absolute values are equal: the insides are equal or opposite
Split into the two cases of the absolute value
Raise the base to the power of both sides
Check the solutions in the original equation
No rule solves this exactly: everything to one side, f(x) = 0
There is no real solution: this can never be true
The two sides are never equal: there is no solution
A product is zero if one of its factors is zero
Solve one of the equations for a variable
Write it into the other equations
Multiply the equations so that a variable has the same coefficient
Both sides are equal for every value
There are no steps for this calculation.

SI: m, kg, m³, N, Pa, J, K, …
US: ft, lb, US gal, psi, …
The middle value once sorted; with an even count, the average of the two middle ones
How spread out a sample is (divides by n − 1)
How spread out a whole population is (divides by n)
The square of stdev (sample, divides by n − 1)
The square of stdevp (population, divides by n)
How precise the mean of a sample is: s/√n
nCr(n, k): ways to pick k of n items, order does not matter. nCr(5, 2) = 10
nPr(n, k): ways to pick k of n items in order. nPr(5, 2) = 20
The largest number that divides all values: gcd(12, 18) = 6
The smallest number all values divide: lcm(4, 6) = 12
To the nearest whole number; halves go away from 0: round(2.5) = 3
round(x, n): x rounded to n decimal places
Down to a whole number: floor(−2.3) = −3
Up to a whole number: ceil(2.1) = 3
The most frequent value; the first of them if there is a tie
The largest minus the smallest value
Adds the values you list: sum(2, 4, 9) = 15. For a sum with an index, use the Σ key
Multiplies the values you list: prod(2, 4, 9) = 72. For a product with an index, long press Σ
Adds the squares of the values: sumsq(1, 2, 3) = 14
percentile(p, values…): the value that p percent of the data lie below (p from 0 to 100)
quartile(q, values…): q = 1, 2 or 3 for the quartiles (2 is the median); 0 and 4 give min and max
How lopsided the data are: 0 if symmetric, positive if the long tail is on the right. At least 3 values
Margin of error of the mean (t)
tmargin(c, values…): the margin of error of the mean at confidence c (0.95 for 95 percent); the interval is mean ± margin
tstat(μ₀, values…): the t value of a one-sample t test against the mean μ₀
Ways to split k₁ + k₂ + … items into groups of k₁, k₂, … items: multinomial(2, 1) = 3
fib(n): the n-th Fibonacci number (0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …): fib(10) = 55
The smallest prime above n: nextprime(10) = 11
1 if n is a prime, otherwise 0
φ(n): how many of 1 … n share no factor with n: totient(9) = 6
Splits a whole number into primes: factor(360) = 2³ × 3² × 5
Multiplies out products and powers: expand((x + 1)²) = x² + 2x + 1
Splits a fraction of polynomials into simpler fractions: apart(1/(x² − 1)) = 1/(2(x − 1)) − 1/(2(x + 1))
taylor(f, x, a, n): a polynomial up to xⁿ that approximates f near x = a

A differential equation: wanted is a function y(x) for which y and its derivatives (y′ = dy/dx, y″ = d²y/dx²) make the equation true for every x. The solution has free constants C, since such an equation has many solutions

An initial value problem: wanted is a function y(x) for which y and its derivatives (y′ = dy/dx, y″ = d²y/dx²) make the equation true for every x, and which takes the given initial values. First the general solution, then the constants for the initial values
Type: first-order, separable. The right side is a function of x times a function of y, so the variables can be separated
Type: first-order, linear. y and y′ appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together; in standard form it is solved with an integrating factor
Type: second-order, linear with constant coefficients, homogeneous (the right side is 0). It is solved with the characteristic equation

Type: second-order, linear with constant coefficients, inhomogeneous (the right side r(x) is not 0). Solution = general solution yₕ of the homogeneous equation (right side 0) + one particular solution yₚ
Multiply by μ: the left side is (μ·y)′. Integrate both sides
Separate the variables: write y′ as dy/dx, divide by g(y) and multiply by dx, so that y is only on the left and x only on the right
Integrate both sides: the left side with respect to y, the right side with respect to x
Work out both integrals. The two constants of integration are combined into one constant C on the right
Drop the absolute value: the sign ± goes into the constant. ±e^C is again an arbitrary constant, so it is called C again
The constant part is again an arbitrary constant: it is called C again
Try y = e^(rx): put y, y′ = r·e^(rx) and y″ = r²·e^(rx) into the equation
Divide by e^(rx), which is never 0. What is left is the characteristic equation, a quadratic equation in r
Solve the characteristic equation with the quadratic formula
Two different real roots r₁ and r₂: e^(r₁x) and e^(r₂x) are both solutions. The general solution combines them
A double root r: e^(rx) and x·e^(rx) are both solutions. The general solution combines them
Complex roots α ± βi: e^(αx)·cos(βx) and e^(αx)·sin(βx) are both real solutions. The general solution combines them
Find a particular solution by variation of parameters (W is the Wronskian)
Find a particular solution: a guess of the same kind as the right side (times x if it solves the equation without the right side), with the coefficients worked out
Choose the constants so that the initial conditions hold
Differentiate the general solution: the condition on y′ needs y′
Insert the initial values into the general solution
Put the constants into the general solution: this is the solution of the initial value problem
Raise both sides to the power 1/n
Apply the inverse function to both sides
dsolve(equation): solves y′ = 2x·y and the like; type y′ as d/dx(y) (long press ∫dx)
modpow(b, e, m): bᵉ mod m, also for huge powers
Drops the decimals: trunc(−2.7) = −2. trunc(x, n) keeps n of them
Only the decimals, with the sign: frac(−2.75) = −0.75
−1, 0 or 1 for a negative number, zero or a positive number
The angle to the positive real axis, in radians from −π to π: arg(i) = π/2
Flips the sign of the imaginary part: conj(3 + 4i) = 3 − 4i
The factorial for any number: Γ(n + 1) = n!, Γ(0.5) = √π
ln Γ(x) for x > 0, for when Γ(x) itself is too large
ψ(x) = Γ′(x)/Γ(x), the derivative of ln Γ(x)
2/√π · ∫₀ˣ e^(−t²) dt, the basis of the normal distribution
1 − erf(x), accurate also for large x
gammainc(a, x): the regularized lower incomplete gamma P(a, x), for a > 0 and x ≥ 0
betainc(x, a, b): the regularized incomplete beta Iₓ(a, b), for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and a, b > 0
The w with w·eʷ = x, for x ≥ −1/e. Solves x·eˣ = 5: x = lambertw(5)
Si(x) = ∫₀ˣ sin(t)/t dt, the antiderivative of sin(x)/x
Ci(x), the antiderivative of cos(x)/x, for x ≠ 0
Ei(x), the antiderivative of eˣ/x, for x ≠ 0
normalpdf(x, μ, σ): the height of the bell curve at x. Without μ and σ: the standard normal distribution
normalcdf(x, μ, σ): the probability of a value up to x. Without μ and σ: the standard normal distribution
normalinv(p, μ, σ): the x that a value stays below with probability p (0 < p < 1)
binompdf(n, p, k): the probability of exactly k successes in n tries, each with probability p
binomcdf(n, p, k): the probability of at most k successes in n tries, each with probability p
poissonpdf(λ, k): the probability of exactly k events when λ are expected
poissoncdf(λ, k): the probability of at most k events when λ are expected
tpdf(x, df): the density of the t distribution with df degrees of freedom
tcdf(x, df): the probability of a value up to x in the t distribution
tinv(p, df): the x that a value stays below with probability p; the critical value of a t test
chisqpdf(x, df): the density of the chi-square distribution with df degrees of freedom
chisqcdf(x, df): the probability of a value up to x in the chi-square distribution
chisqinv(p, df): the x that a value stays below with probability p; the critical value of a chi-square test
A random number from 0 up to 1 (not 1). It stays the same while you edit the line
randint(a, b): a random whole number from a to b. It stays the same while you edit the line
randnorm(μ, σ): a random number from a normal distribution; without μ and σ the standard one
dot(a, b): the dot product of two vectors, a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + …
cross(a, b): the vector perpendicular to the 3D vectors a and b
The length of a vector, √(a₁² + a₂² + …); the same as |a|
angle(a, b): the angle between two vectors, in the angle unit set above the keypad
proj(a, b): the part of a that points along b
unitvec(a): the vector of length 1 in the direction of a
The bits set in both numbers: and(12, 10) = 8
The bits set in either number: or(12, 10) = 14
The bits set in exactly one: xor(12, 10) = 6
shl(n, k): moves the bits k places left, n·2ᵏ: shl(1, 4) = 16 (also n << k)
shr(n, k): moves the bits k places right: shr(16, 2) = 4 (also n >> k)
Several values are separated by “%1$s”: long press the decimal key for it
Molar volume of ideal gas (0 °C, 1 atm)
Drag to choose the size, lift to insert. A vector is a matrix of one column (or one row)
T stands for the transpose of a matrix
Letters are variables: ab means a · b. A function name and ( such as sin( or mean( starts that function.
Complex numbers are now on. You can switch them off in the settings.
Several lines can\'t be pasted into a fraction, root, …
Save or open line and history
There is a history already. Replace it with the one from the file, or add the file\'s entries below it?

This file is not a saved session

resources.string: Tap the curve to place the cursor
Only the surface is drawn: a 3D graph cannot be combined with other lines
Drag the point along the curve; snaps to highlighted points
Drag along the graph; snaps to highlighted points
Drag a or b; they snap to zeros and intersections
One finger rotates · two fingers move and zoom
New here? Start with the topics at the top. The functions further down each have their syntax and examples.
History, input line, live result and keypad
From top to bottom: the history of your calculations, the input line with its result, and the keypad.
The result is worked out while you type, so there is no need to press anything to see it. Equations are solved, derivatives and integrals worked out the same way.
Press the Enter key (↵) to move the line and its result into the history and start a new line.
If a line cannot be calculated, the reason is shown in red in place of the result.
Swipe sideways for the scientific keys and the tools

The keypad has three pages. It starts on the middle one with the digits. The scientific keys are on the page to the left (swipe right to get there), the tools on the page to the right (swipe left). The dots above the keys show the page you are on, and tapping a dot goes there. On a tablet or an unfolded foldable all three pages are shown side by side.
Digits, the decimal point, and ×10ⁿ for a number in scientific notation (5×10³)
The basic operations. ÷ makes a fraction, with the number before it on top
A pair of parentheses with the cursor inside
Deletes what is before the cursor
Puts the line and its result into the history
Factorial, square, square root and the logarithm to base 10
A matrix or vector (opens a size picker), and the trigonometric functions
Integral, sum, the imaginary unit i and π
The equals sign for equations, the variable x, abc for any other letter (opens the system keyboard), and Euler\'s number e
C clears the line. On an empty line it becomes AC, which also clears the history (you can undo it)
Opens the list of units (km, psi, kWh, …) to put one into the line
Opens the function picker: statistics, combinatorics, rounding, distributions, Taylor polynomials, differential equations and more
Opens the mathematical and physical constants (c, h, G, …)
Draws the line as a graph
The angle unit of sin, cos and tan: radians or degrees. Tap to switch
The number base: DEC for normal numbers, or HEX, OCT and BIN, which turn the left page into programmer keys (A to F, AND, OR, shifts)
Where ln, asin, d/dx, lim, ≤, := and the rest are

Many keys have more functions than their label shows. Keep a key pressed: a popup opens with its other functions. Slide your finger to the one you want and lift it. Lifting without sliding takes the main function.
The small labels in the lower corners of a key show what its popup has; “…” means it has even more. Some popups have a second row above the first, for example the hyperbolic functions above sin.
%, mod and Γ; above them the bitwise AND, OR, XOR and NOT
Any power □ⁿ, and the reciprocal □⁻¹ (also the inverse of a matrix)
The natural logarithm ln, and the logarithm to any base logₙ
Transpose Aᵀ, det, rref and eig; above them the vector functions dot, cross, norm, angle, proj and unitvec
The inverse functions (asin), the reciprocal ones (csc, sec, cot) and their inverses; above them the hyperbolic functions (sinh, asinh, …)
The definite integral with bounds, the derivative d/dx, and the derivative at a point
The product ∏ and the limit lim
A complex number in polar form r∠θ
Infinity ∞, for limits, sums and integrals
:= to define a variable, and < > ≤ ≥ for inequalities
A raised + or −, for a limit from one side (x → 0⁺)
A mixed number (3½), and ÷ as a sign instead of a fraction
The separator between the values of a function, mean(2, 4, 9)
A new line (for a system of equations, or several curves in a graph), and Ans, the last result
The arrow → to convert into another unit
Tap anywhere in the line to put the cursor there. Fractions, powers and roots have boxes (□) for their parts; tap a box or move the cursor into it to fill it in.
Press and hold to select a part of the line, and keep dragging to select more. The handles below a selection adjust it. When you lift your finger, a menu offers Cut, Copy, Paste and Select all.
With something selected, a function key wraps it: select 2x + 1 and tap √□ to get √(2x + 1).
To paste, tap the cursor (or press and hold an empty spot) and choose Paste. Numbers copied from other apps can be pasted.
A system of equations or several graphs are written as several lines: long press Enter and choose “new line”.
Reuse, copy and delete earlier calculations
Tap the calculation of an entry to put it back in the line and change it.
Tap the result of an entry to start a new line with it.
Press and hold a calculation or result to copy it. Swipe an entry sideways to delete it; a message lets you undo that.
Ans (long press Enter) stands for the last result, so 2·Ans doubles it.
Exact or decimal, and the step-by-step solution

Results are exact where possible: fractions, roots and π stay as they are. The buttons next to the result switch between the forms that make sense for it: Exact, Decimal, Sci (scientific notation), Mixed (mixed numbers), Polar (complex numbers) and HEX, OCT, BIN.

Steps opens the step-by-step solution: each step with the rule that was used. Steps are there for equations, systems, inequalities, derivatives, integrals, limits, matrices, Taylor polynomials, differential equations and more.
Press and hold the result to copy it.
x, y, z, any letter, and storing values with :=

The x key types x; long press it for y and z. For any other letter tap abc: the system keyboard opens and types into the line. Letters next to each other are multiplied, so ab means a·b. A function name followed by “(” starts that function, for example sin( or mean(.
Variables are lower-case letters. e, π and i are constants, not variables.
Write a letter, := (long press =) and a value, and press Enter. From then on the letter has this value in every line.
This also stores matrices and vectors, for example m := a matrix, so you can use m in the next lines. Delete the line from the history to forget the value.

The Func key on the right page opens all functions that have no key of their own, sorted by topic. Search for a name or a word of its description. Each entry tells what the function does and how it is written.
Tapping one puts it into the line with the cursor inside. Values are separated with the separator: long press the decimal point key for it.
If you select values first (2, 4, 9) and then pick a function, it takes them.
Solve for x, systems of equations, inequalities
Type an equation with the = key (left page). It is solved for its variable while you type.
Write each equation on its own line: long press Enter and choose “new line” between them. Linear and many non-linear systems are solved.
Long press = for <, >, ≤ and ≥. The solution is also given in interval notation and on a number line in the steps.
d/dx, the derivative at a point, partial derivatives
Long press ∫dx (left page) and choose d/dx, then type the function inside.
For the value of the derivative at a point, choose the third entry of the popup, d/dx with x = a, and fill in the point.
To differentiate by another variable, tap the x of dx and type the letter. With a second variable in the function the derivative is a partial one and is written ∂/∂x.
Tap ∫dx (left page) for an antiderivative and type the function inside.
For a definite integral, long press ∫dx and choose the one with bounds; fill in the lower and upper bound. ∞ (long press π) works as a bound.
Tap the x of dx to integrate over another variable. A definite integral that has no formula is worked out numerically.
Σ, ∏, lim, and sum or prod of a list
Tap Σ (left page) for a sum: fill in the index with its start (n = 1), the end and the term. Long press Σ for the product ∏.
Long press Σ and choose lim for a limit: fill in the point after the arrow and the function.
The raised + (long press +) makes it a limit from the right
taylor(f, x, a, n): a function as a polynomial around a point
taylor gives the Taylor polynomial of a function: the polynomial that matches the function and its first n derivatives at the point a. Near a it is a good approximation of the function.
Func (right page) → Calculus → Taylor polynomial. Or tap abc and type taylor( .
Around 0, in the only variable of f, up to the power n
In the variable x, around 0, up to the power n. Needed when f has several variables
In x around the point a, up to the power n. a is a number or a constant such as π
Around a = 1 it is written in powers of (x − 1)
n is a whole number from 0 to 12.
f and its derivatives must be defined at a: taylor(ln(x), x, 0, 3) or taylor(sin(x)/x, x, 0, 4) give an error. Choose another point, or simplify f first.

The result is a polynomial you can work with: differentiate or integrate it, or draw it together with f in the graph (each on its own line) to see where it is close. Steps shows the whole way: the Taylor formula for n, the derivatives, their values at a, the values put in, and the simplified polynomial.
dsolve: ordinary differential equations of first and second order
dsolve solves an ordinary differential equation for the unknown function y(x): it gives the general solution with constants C (C₁, C₂), or, with initial conditions, the one solution that meets them.
Func (right page) → Calculus → Differential equation. Or tap abc and type dsolve( .

y′ is written with the derivative key: long press ∫dx and choose d/dx, then type y (long press x). For y″ put a d/dx inside a d/dx. The = is the key on the left page, and the commas before the conditions come from a long press on the decimal point key.
First order, with the initial condition y(x₀) = y₀
Second order, with the conditions y(x₀) = y₀ and y′(x₀) = y′₀

First order: linear equations a·y′ + b·y = c, where a, b and c may depend on x, and separable equations y′ = f(x)·g(y). When a separable equation cannot be solved for y, the solution is given as an equation in x and y. An equation that is both, such as y′ = 3x·y, is solved by separating the variables, as in most textbooks.
Second order: a·y″ + b·y′ + c·y = r(x) with numbers a, b, c. The right side r(x) can be 0, or made of polynomials, eᵏˣ, sin and cos.
Every solution is checked by putting it back into the equation. Equations of other kinds (y′ = y² + x, y″ with non-constant coefficients, third order) are not solved and give a message.

The unknown may have another letter than y, and the variable is x unless you tap the x of dx to change it. Steps shows the method: separating the variables, the integrating factor, or the characteristic equation.
Size picker, det, inverse, eigenvalues, vector functions

Tap the matrix key (left page, the bracketed grid). Drag across the grid to choose the size and lift your finger to insert it, or choose a 2D or 3D vector. A vector is a matrix with one column (or one row).

Matrices are added, subtracted and multiplied with the usual keys. Long press the matrix key for the transpose, det, rref (row reduction) and eig (eigenvalues and eigenvectors). The inverse is □⁻¹ (long press □²).
The upper row of the popup has the vector functions: dot and cross product, norm, the angle between two vectors, projection and unit vector.
To use a matrix again, store it with := (see Variables). Lines with a parameter, (1, 2) + r·(2, 1), can be drawn in the graph.
Tap i (left page) to type the imaginary unit; this turns complex numbers on in the settings. Long press i for the polar form r∠θ.
The Polar button next to a complex result shows it as r∠θ. The function picker has re, im, arg and conj under Complex numbers.
Calculate with units, convert, physical constants
Tap Units (right page) and search for a unit to put it after a number. Calculations with units keep track of them, and results are shown in the unit system of the settings.
To convert, long press Units for the arrow →, then put the target unit after it.
Const (right page) has mathematical and physical constants with their units, such as the speed of light c or Planck\'s constant h. Search by name or symbol and tap one to insert it.
Type a function and tap Graph (right page). Several lines become several curves, and where they cross is marked.
An equation in x and y: a circle
A function of x and y is drawn as a 3D surface
Pinch to zoom and drag to move. Tap a curve to place a point on it; it snaps to zeros, maxima, minima, inflection points and intersections.
The graph tools: Trace follows the curve, Tangent shows the slope at the point, Integral shows the area between two bounds a and b. The axes menu has logarithmic axes and polar coordinates.
To add a curve, use “Add another equation”; each curve can be hidden and shown again. A 3D surface turns with one finger and moves and zooms with two.

Tap DEC above the keypad and choose HEX, OCT or BIN. The digit keys then type in that base, and the left page has the digits A to F and the bitwise keys AND, OR, XOR, NOT and the shifts << and >>. Numbers get their prefix by themselves (0x, 0o, 0b), and results are shown in the base.
Back in DEC, the result buttons HEX, OCT and BIN still show a whole number in the other bases.

Settings → Session → Save… writes the line and the whole history to a text file, for example to keep a set of calculations or move it to another device. Open… reads such a file back: replace the history with it, or add its entries below.
For a list of numbers there is no need for an index: sum and prod in the function picker (Func → Statistics) add up or multiply the values you list.
Find out where each function is and how to use it. The help is also in the settings.
